title: Facet Joint Pain & Medial Branch Blocks

sections.title: Technique & Approach
sections.content:
## Medial Branch Block Technique

Medial branch blocks (MBBs) are the reference standard for diagnosing facet-mediated pain. The technique targets the small medial branch nerves of the dorsal rami that innervate the facet joints.

### Understanding Dual Innervation

Each lumbar facet joint receives innervation from **two medial branch nerves**:
- The medial branch at the same level as the superior articular process
- The medial branch from one level above

**Example**: The L4-5 facet joint is innervated by:
- The **L3 medial branch** (courses over the L4 transverse process)
- The **L4 medial branch** (courses over the L5 transverse process)

**Practical implication**: To completely block or denervate a single facet joint, **two nerves must be targeted**.

**Special case — L5-S1**: Innervated by the L4 medial branch and the **L5 dorsal ramus** (not a medial branch — the L5 dorsal ramus has a different anatomical course along the ala of the sacrum).

### Anatomical Targets

- **L1-L4 medial branches**: Target is the junction of the transverse process and the superior articular process (SAP) at the level below (e.g., L3 medial branch targeted at junction of L4 TP and L4 SAP)
- **L5 dorsal ramus**: Target is the junction of the S1 SAP and the sacral ala
- **Cervical medial branches**: Course over the waist of the articular pillar at each level — more consistent anatomy than lumbar

### Cervical MBB Technique Details (IPSIS)

Cervical medial branch anatomy and blocking technique differ from the lumbar spine in important ways:

#### Third Occipital Nerve (TON) — C2-3 Joint
- The C2-3 joint is **uniquely innervated by the TON** (superficial medial branch of the C3 dorsal ramus), not by a typical medial branch pair
- The TON varies in position from superior to inferior along the lateral C2-3 joint, so **three target points** are used along the longitudinal bisector of the joint (at the C3 SAP apex, base, and equator)
- Total local anesthetic volume for a 3-injection TON block: **0.6 mL (0.2 mL per target)**
- Contrast use is prudent at the TON level given the possibility of aberrant vertebral artery loops near the target

#### Typical Cervical Levels (C3-6)
- The medial branches course along the **waist (concavity) of their respective articular pillars**
- The target is the **centroid** of the articular pillar — the intersection of two diagonals of the diamond-shaped pillar
- A **single block point** at the centroid is sufficient to anesthetize the medial branch at each typical level
- Recommended local anesthetic volume: **0.25 mL** per level (lower than older protocols that used 0.5 mL, to improve diagnostic specificity)
- True lateral segmental imaging is essential — the bilateral articular pillars must be superimposed for accurate target identification

#### C7 Medial Branch
- The C7 medial branch is **not associated with an articular pillar** but crosses the C7 SAP or the base of the C7 transverse process
- Its variable location requires **three target points**: SAP apex, SAP base near the TP junction, and a third point slightly superficial to the SAP apex
- Total local anesthetic volume: **0.6 mL (0.2 mL at each of three targets)**
- Contrast is optional at C7 because multiple injections are performed, and residual contrast from one target may obscure subsequent placements

#### Patient Positioning for Cervical MBBs
- **Lateral approach**: patient may be lateral decubitus (target side up), supine, or prone with a laterally positioned fluoroscope
- **Posterior approach**: patient prone with chest bolster to flex the neck; fluoroscope is declined caudally to reveal the articular pillar waists (pillar view)

### Lumbar MBB Technique Details (IPSIS)

#### Anatomy and Target Acquisition — L1-4 Medial Branches
- The bony target lies **one-third to one-half the distance** along an imaginary line from the inflection (curve between SAP base and TP) to the mamillary process
- The SAP is often angled from medial to lateral in the axial plane, which requires **ipsilateral fluoroscopic obliquity** (typically 30-40 degrees) to access the medial branch without the needle being deflected laterally by an overhanging dorsal SAP
- Bulbous (mushroom-shaped) SAPs from osteoarthritic changes may demand additional obliquity
- The **mamillo-accessory ligament (MAL)** covers the nerve at L1-4 levels — if the needle sits atop the MAL rather than beneath it, anesthetic may not reach the target, causing a false-negative block

#### L5 Dorsal Ramus Target
- The L5 dorsal ramus is targeted in the **groove (sulcus) between the S1 SAP base and the sacral ala**
- There is no MAL at S1
- A high-riding iliac crest may obstruct access; increasing the cephalad fluoroscopic tilt to square off the S1 endplate usually displaces the crest enough
- The needle must never stray cephalad to the S1 SAP/sacral ala notch (risking the L5 nerve root) or too far inferiorly toward the posterior S1 foramen

#### Lumbar Injectate Volumes
- Contrast: 0.1-0.3 mL to confirm spread and rule out venous uptake
- Local anesthetic: **0.25-0.5 mL** per nerve (volumes as low as 0.25 mL may be sufficient)
- A declined fluoroscopic view helps confirm that contrast fills the notch between the SAP and TP

### Thoracic MBB Considerations (IPSIS)

Thoracic medial branch procedures remain an area of evolving understanding:
- Recent anatomic studies have challenged the traditional assumption that thoracic facet joint articular branches arise from the distal medial branch (as in the lumbar spine)
- Multiple cadaveric dissections have found that articular branches at T1-9 frequently arise directly from the dorsal ramus or very proximal medial branch, near the neural foramen — not from the distal medial branch where blocks and RF lesions are traditionally placed
- At T10, the medial branch crosses the superolateral corner of the transverse process in about 70% of specimens (and just cranial to it in 30%)
- At T11, the course is more constant over the superolateral TP corner
- At T12, the anatomy resembles the lumbar medial branch pattern
- Despite these anatomic uncertainties, if diagnostic TMBBs achieve 80-100% relief, it is reasonable to expect that radiofrequency coagulation at the same site would extend that pain relief

### Step-by-Step Technique (General)

1. **Patient positioning**: Prone on fluoroscopy table
2. **Level identification**: AP fluoroscopy to identify target transverse processes
3. **Needle placement**: 22-25 gauge spinal needle advanced to the junction of the TP and SAP under fluoroscopic guidance
4. **Confirm position**: AP and lateral views to verify needle tip at the target
5. **Contrast injection**: Small volume (0.1-0.3 mL) to check spread — ensures contrast stays at the target and does not spread to adjacent structures or show venous uptake
6. **Anesthetic injection**: **0.25-0.5 mL** of local anesthetic per nerve (lumbar); **0.25 mL** per level (cervical typical); **0.2 mL per target** (cervical TON/C7)
   - First block: Typically bupivacaine 0.5%
   - Confirmatory block: Lidocaine 2% (on a separate day)
7. **Multiple levels**: Repeat for each medial branch nerve that must be blocked
8. **Post-procedure assessment**: Evaluate the patient for 20-60 minutes for degree of pain relief and response to previously painful activity; provide a pain diary

### Controlled (Dual) Block Protocol

1. **First MBB**: Using one anesthetic (e.g., bupivacaine 0.5%)
2. **Assessment**: Patient must report **>80% pain relief** lasting an appropriate duration
3. **Second MBB** (confirmatory): On a **separate day**, using a different anesthetic (e.g., lidocaine 2%)
4. **Concordant response**: Relief duration must correspond to the pharmacology of the anesthetic — shorter with lidocaine, longer with bupivacaine
5. **If both positive**: Patient is a candidate for radiofrequency ablation
keyPoints: Each facet joint is innervated by TWO medial branch nerves — both must be blocked for complete anesthesia
L5-S1 is a special case: innervated by L4 medial branch and L5 dorsal ramus (different anatomical course)
Use 0.5 mL per nerve — small volumes maintain diagnostic specificity
Controlled (dual) blocks with different anesthetics on separate days reduce false positive rate from 25-40% to 5-10%
Concordant response means relief duration matches the expected pharmacology of each anesthetic
10-15% of the time, contrast check reveals the medication is not reaching the target — always use contrast
Cervical medial branches have more consistent anatomy at the waist of the articular pillar
Cervical typical levels (C3-6): target the centroid of the articular pillar using 0.25 mL anesthetic; lower volumes improve specificity (IPSIS)
The TON and C7 medial branch each require THREE target points due to anatomic variability (IPSIS)
Lumbar MBBs require ipsilateral obliquity (typically 30-40 degrees) to access the medial branch beneath the SAP (IPSIS)
The mamillo-accessory ligament covers L1-4 medial branches — needle placement atop the MAL causes false-negative blocks (IPSIS)
True lateral segmental imaging is essential for cervical MBBs — superimpose the bilateral articular pillars at each level (IPSIS)
Vascular uptake occurs in up to 6% of cervical MBBs — always use contrast and real-time fluoroscopy to detect it (IPSIS)
Post-procedure: evaluate patient 20-60 minutes for pain relief and response to previously painful activity; provide a pain diary (IPSIS)
Thoracic medial branch anatomy is evolving — recent studies show articular branches may arise from the dorsal ramus rather than the distal medial branch (IPSIS)
Adjacent to a posterolateral fusion construct, the medial branch at the fused level is already destroyed and does not need to be targeted (IPSIS)

sections.title: Clinical Decision-Making
sections.content:
## Identifying Facet Pain Candidates

### Clinical Presentation

Facet joint pain is an **axial pain generator** — it produces back or neck pain but should NOT cause radicular symptoms below the knee (lumbar) or below the shoulder (cervical).

**Suggestive features** (none are diagnostic alone):
- Paraspinal tenderness over the facet joints
- Pain with spinal extension and ipsilateral rotation
- Absence of radicular features (no dermatomal pain below the knee or shoulder)
- Pain that is predominantly one-sided but can be bilateral
- Pain referral patterns overlap with other structures (disc, SI joint, myofascial)

### The Dreyfuss Teaching Point

Paul Dreyfuss's landmark 1997 study established a critical principle: **no single historical or physical examination finding reliably diagnoses facet joint pain**. This means:
- Clinical features are **suggestive but not diagnostic**
- Controlled medial branch blocks are the **reference standard** for diagnosis
- You cannot diagnose facet pain on history and exam alone

### Age Considerations

Age is an important factor in clinical decision-making:

- **Under 35 years**: Facet joint degeneration is uncommon. Facet pain in young patients should raise suspicion for other diagnoses (disc pathology, spondylolysis, inflammatory spondyloarthropathy)
- **Why <35 is rarely appropriate**: The degenerative cascade (Kirkaldy-Willis) typically begins in the 4th-5th decades. Treating young patients with MBBs and RFA without strong diagnostic suspicion raises appropriateness concerns.
- **Peak prevalence**: 40-70 years, correlating with progressive facet arthropathy
- **Elderly patients**: High prevalence of imaging arthropathy, but correlation with pain is imperfect

### Prevalence Data

- **Lumbar facet pain**: ~27-41% of chronic low back pain populations
- **Cervical facet pain**: ~36-67% of chronic neck pain, particularly post-whiplash
- **Overall**: Facet joint pain accounts for approximately 15-45% of chronic back pain

### Insurance and Documentation Requirements

- **Medicare LCD**: Most require dual comparative blocks before approving RFA
- **Documentation needed**: Specific pain relief percentage, duration of relief, functional improvement
- **Relief threshold**: Some payers require >80% on both blocks; others accept >50%
- **Blocks must be on separate dates**
- **Maximum levels**: 2-3 levels per session is typical coverage
- **Conservative care failure**: Must document failed PT, medications, etc.

### Facet Injection vs Medial Branch Block

- **Intra-articular facet injections** are primarily therapeutic (steroid delivery) and less reliable diagnostically than MBBs
- **MBBs** are the diagnostic reference standard because they specifically test the innervation pathway that would be ablated with RFA
- MBBs are prognostic: a positive block predicts response to RFA
- IPSIS notes that facet joint capsules are often fenestrated — intra-articular anesthetic can leak to the epidural space or other structures, reducing diagnostic specificity

### Pre-Procedure Imaging (IPSIS)

- Pre-procedure review of advanced imaging (CT/MRI) is recommended to enhance procedural planning
- However, imaging is **neither sensitive nor specific** for diagnosing facet joint pain — there is no reliable correlation between the imaging appearance of a facet joint and facet-mediated pain
- Facet pain may coexist with disc herniations or other abnormalities visible on imaging
- In the cervical spine, common imaging studies often fail to detect facet joint injury after whiplash
- The diagnosis of facet pain depends on the patient's response to properly performed MBBs, not imaging findings

### Procedure-Specific Contraindications (IPSIS)

- All general contraindications to interventional spine procedures apply (see fundamentals): active systemic infection, inability to provide consent, pregnancy, uncontrolled coagulopathy
- Structural or anatomic abnormalities that compromise safe needle placement are procedure-specific contraindications
- In cervical procedures, pre-procedure imaging should screen for aberrant vertebral artery loops, especially at C2-3
- Patients on antithrombotic therapy require careful risk-benefit assessment per IPSIS antithrombotics guidelines

### Fusion Construct Considerations (IPSIS)

- Standard posterolateral lumbar fusions inherently destroy the medial branch at each fused level through surgical exposure, decortication, pedicle screw placement, and bone grafting
- When evaluating a joint adjacent to a fusion, only the unfused medial branch needs targeting
- Example: if fusion spans L2-4, only the L4 medial branch (not L3) needs to be blocked to evaluate the L4-5 facet joint
keyPoints: Facet pain is axial — it should NOT cause radicular symptoms below the knee (lumbar) or shoulder (cervical)
No single exam finding reliably diagnoses facet pain (Dreyfuss 1997) — controlled blocks are the reference standard
Age matters: facet pain in patients under 35 is uncommon and should raise suspicion for other diagnoses
Peak prevalence is 40-70 years, correlating with the degenerative cascade
Lumbar facet pain accounts for 27-41% of chronic low back pain
Medicare typically requires dual comparative blocks on separate days before approving RFA
MBBs are prognostic for RFA response; intra-articular facet injections are less reliable diagnostically
Imaging is neither sensitive nor specific for facet pain — no reliable correlation between facet joint appearance and pain (IPSIS)
Facet joint capsules are often fenestrated, allowing intra-articular anesthetic to leak and reduce diagnostic specificity (IPSIS)
When a posterolateral fusion exists, the medial branch at the fused level is already destroyed surgically (IPSIS)
Screen for aberrant vertebral artery loops before cervical procedures, especially at C2-3 (IPSIS)

sections.title: Evidence & Guidelines
sections.content:
## Foundational Research

### Dreyfuss P et al. (1997) — Spine

This landmark study established the foundation for modern facet pain diagnosis:
- Demonstrated that **no single historical or physical examination finding** reliably diagnoses facet joint pain
- Challenged the notion that facet pain could be diagnosed clinically
- **Established the need for controlled diagnostic blocks** as the reference standard
- Clinical features (paraspinal tenderness, extension pain) are suggestive but not diagnostic

### False Positive Rate of Single Blocks

- **Schwarzer AC et al. (1994)**: Single medial branch blocks have a false positive rate of approximately **25-40%**
- **Manchikanti L et al. (2004)**: Confirmed the high false positive rate and established the need for controlled blocks
- **Controlled blocks reduce false positive rate to approximately 5-10%** and significantly increase diagnostic specificity

### Prevalence Studies

- **Manchikanti L et al. (2004)**: Lumbar facet pain prevalence of 27-41% in chronic LBP populations using controlled diagnostic blocks
- **Schwarzer AC et al. (1995)**: Similar prevalence data in chronic low back pain
- **Barnsley L et al. (1995)**: Cervical facet pain prevalence of 54% in chronic neck pain, particularly post-whiplash
- **Lord SM et al. (1996)**: Confirmed high prevalence of cervical facet pain as a cause of post-whiplash headache

### Why Controlled Blocks Matter

The dual block paradigm is supported by strong evidence:
1. **False positive rate of single blocks is 25-40%** — unacceptably high for guiding treatment
2. **Concordant response validation**: Using two different anesthetics with different durations provides internal validation
3. **Insurance alignment**: Medicare LCDs require dual blocks before RFA approval
4. **Better RFA outcomes**: Patients selected with controlled blocks have significantly better RFA outcomes than those selected with single blocks

## Guidelines

- **SIS**: Recommends controlled (dual) medial branch blocks as the diagnostic standard for facet pain
- **ASIPP**: Level I-II evidence for medial branch blocks in diagnosing facet-mediated pain
- **Medicare LCD**: Requires dual comparative blocks before RFA; documentation of relief percentage, duration, and functional improvement
- **SPECT scanning**: May increase pre-test probability by showing active facet arthropathy — a useful adjunct but not diagnostic alone

## IPSIS Consensus and Technical Guidance (2024)

### Key IPSIS Technical Points for MBBs

- **Noncomparative dual blocks may be sufficient**: While comparative blocks (using two different anesthetics) have traditionally been recommended, IPSIS acknowledges that noncomparative dual blocks may be adequate for diagnosing facet-mediated pain
- **80-100% relief threshold**: A positive diagnostic block requires at least 80% pain relief lasting for the minimum expected duration of the anesthetic used
- **False-positive rate of single blocks**: Confirmed at 25-45%, reinforcing the need for dual blocks with small volumes
- **Volume matters for specificity**: Lower anesthetic volumes (0.25 mL for lumbar, 0.25 mL for cervical typical levels) are now recommended over earlier higher-volume protocols to prevent spread to adjacent pain-generating structures
- **Contrast medium is essential**: Used to rule out vascular uptake (up to 6% of cervical cases) and to verify adequate spread to the nerve target
- **Fluoroscopy remains the preferred guidance modality**: The IPSIS Patient Safety Committee has questioned the safety and efficacy of ultrasound guidance for cervical spine procedures
keyPoints: Dreyfuss (1997): No single clinical finding reliably diagnoses facet pain — controlled blocks are the standard
Single block false positive rate is 25-40% (Schwarzer 1994) — unacceptably high for treatment decisions
Controlled blocks reduce false positive rate to 5-10% using concordant response validation
Lumbar facet pain prevalence: 27-41% of chronic LBP (Manchikanti 2004)
Cervical facet pain prevalence: 36-67% of chronic neck pain, higher in post-whiplash (Barnsley 1995)
Patients selected with controlled blocks have significantly better RFA outcomes
SPECT scanning can increase pre-test probability but is not diagnostic alone
IPSIS (2024): noncomparative dual blocks may be sufficient — comparative blocks are not strictly required
IPSIS recommends lower anesthetic volumes (0.25 mL lumbar, 0.25 mL cervical) to improve diagnostic specificity
Fluoroscopy is the preferred imaging modality for MBBs — IPSIS questions safety/efficacy of ultrasound guidance for cervical procedures

sections.title: UpToDate: Facet Diagnosis & MBB Evidence Context
sections.content:
## UpToDate Perspective on Facet Joint Pain Diagnosis

UpToDate adds important evidence context regarding the diagnostic workup for facet-mediated pain, the limitations of imaging, and the role of intra-articular facet injections as an alternative in select populations.

### 80% Pain Relief Threshold as the Recommended Standard

UpToDate reinforces that the relief threshold used for diagnostic medial branch blocks directly affects treatment outcomes. The 80% pain relief threshold is the widely accepted standard for determining a positive diagnostic block. Studies using a lower 50% threshold have produced worse outcomes in subsequent radiofrequency ablation, contributing to controversial negative trials such as the MINT trial. UpToDate's framing aligns with both IPSIS and the Cohen (2010) data showing that the rigor of diagnostic block criteria is the strongest predictor of RFA success.

### Medial Branch Blocks for Cervical AND Lumbar Facet Pain

UpToDate discusses RFA and its prerequisite diagnostic blocks in the context of both cervical and lumbar facet pain. The medial branch block paradigm applies across spinal regions — not just the lumbar spine. For cervical facet pain, which accounts for a substantial proportion of chronic neck pain (especially post-whiplash), the same dual-block diagnostic approach is recommended before proceeding to cervical medial branch radiofrequency neurotomy.

### Intra-Articular Facet Injection: Limited but Potential Role in Younger Patients

While UpToDate and UK NICE guidelines generally recommend against facet joint glucocorticoid injections for chronic nonradicular low back pain due to limited evidence of sustained benefit and risk of harm, there may be a clinical role for intra-articular facet injections as a therapeutic option in younger patients (under age 50) who are not yet candidates for denervation. In this population, delivering steroid directly to an inflamed facet joint can provide symptomatic relief without committing to the RFA pathway. However, the diagnostic specificity of intra-articular injection is inferior to MBBs because fenestrated joint capsules allow anesthetic leakage to adjacent structures.

### Facet Arthropathy: Weak Imaging-Clinical Correlation

UpToDate highlights a critical limitation: the correlation between imaging findings of facet arthropathy (joint space narrowing, osteophytes, sclerosis, inflammatory changes) and the patient's actual response to facet blocks is weak. Facet arthropathy is common on imaging in asymptomatic individuals, especially with advancing age. Because imaging cannot reliably distinguish painful from painless facet joints, the diagnosis of facet-mediated pain ultimately depends on the patient's response to properly performed medial branch blocks — not on the radiologic appearance of the joints. This reinforces the Dreyfuss (1997) principle that no single clinical or imaging finding reliably diagnoses facet pain.

### Sedation Discouraged During Diagnostic MBBs

For procedures that depend on assessing the patient's pain response — including medial branch blocks — UpToDate discourages sedation because it increases the false-positive rate of diagnostic blocks. This is consistent with IPSIS guidance requiring patients to remain conscious and conversant.

### UpToDate Does NOT Recommend Facet or Medial Branch Glucocorticoid Injections

Notably, UpToDate explicitly recommends against glucocorticoid injections at facet joints and medial branches for chronic nonradicular low back pain, citing limited evidence of benefit, no evidence of long-term benefit, and risk of serious harm. UK NICE guidelines similarly recommend against these injections. The distinction is important: MBBs with local anesthetic for diagnostic purposes remain the standard, but steroid injections at these targets for therapeutic purposes are not supported by the evidence base.
keyPoints: The 80% pain relief threshold is the recommended standard for a positive diagnostic MBB — lower thresholds yield worse RFA outcomes (UpToDate)
The MBB diagnostic paradigm applies to both cervical and lumbar facet pain — cervical facet pain is especially common post-whiplash (UpToDate)
Intra-articular facet injection may have a therapeutic role in younger patients (<50) not yet candidates for denervation, but its diagnostic specificity is inferior to MBBs (UpToDate)
The correlation between imaging findings of facet arthropathy and response to facet blocks is weak — imaging cannot distinguish painful from painless facet joints (UpToDate)
Sedation during diagnostic MBBs increases the false-positive rate and is discouraged (UpToDate)
UpToDate and UK NICE recommend AGAINST facet joint and medial branch glucocorticoid injections for chronic nonradicular LBP — limited benefit, no long-term evidence, risk of harm
MBBs with local anesthetic for diagnosis remain the standard; the evidence does not support steroid injections at these targets therapeutically (UpToDate)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (Dr. O'Brien)
sections.content:
## Dr. O'Brien on Facet Pain and Medial Branch Blocks

### Understanding the Anatomy

Dr. O'Brien teaches the anatomy in practical terms. The nerves that come off the nerve root are named after the nerve root, not the spinal segment level. If the L3 nerve root gives off the L3 dorsal ramus and medial branch, that medial branch goes back to innervate the facet joint. When someone has bad facet pain, they can actually have pain radiating down their leg — not because the nerve root is compressed, but because the pain signal travels back through the same dorsal root ganglion to the brain. This is referred pain, just like people having a heart attack experience jaw or arm pain.

### Age-Based Clinical Suspicion

Dr. O'Brien has a clear framework for age-based suspicion of facet pain. He rarely looks at someone under 35 and considers RFA just because they have back pain — their MRIs are usually normal. He has seen many 20-year-olds undergoing medial branch blocks with pristine imaging, which he questions. What are you going to do — perform RFA every six months for the next 30 years?

The exception is when a young patient has a genuinely arthritic facet joint from a sports injury or trauma. But the default for young patients should be to look for other diagnoses first.

Facet pain prevalence increases significantly as patients get older, especially above age 50. As discs collapse with age, more weight transfers to the facet joints — from about 25% of body weight when younger to 50% around age 50.

### Why MBBs Over Intra-Articular Injection for Diagnosis

Dr. O'Brien explains that the trouble with injecting into the joint for diagnostic purposes is that you cannot be sure you are anesthetizing the whole joint complex. Paul Dreyfuss and others showed that blocking the innervation of the joint (via MBBs) is more specific. And it is prognostic — if blocking the nerve takes away the pain, then killing the nerve with RFA should take away the pain.

There is still a role for intra-articular facet injections therapeutically — for example, when a patient has a big effusion around the facet joint that needs steroid treatment, or for facet cyst rupture. But for diagnostic purposes, MBBs are the standard.

### Contrast Is Essential

Dr. O'Brien emphasizes that 10 to 15% of the time, if you do not check contrast before injecting the anesthetic, the medication gets washed away from the target. Any provider sending patients for medial branch blocks without using contrast should be viewed as a red flag — unless the patient has a true contrast allergy.

### The Ethical Dimension

Dr. O'Brien shares an example of a nurse practitioner who told a patient their pain was from the SI joint — without even examining the SI joint — but then ordered medial branch blocks because the patient's insurance would not cover SI joint procedures. He uses examples like this to teach fellows about the importance of matching the diagnosis to the procedure and maintaining ethical practice.
keyPoints: Facet pain can cause referred leg pain through the dorsal root ganglion — like cardiac referred pain to the jaw
Rarely consider RFA in patients under 35 — their facets are usually normal and other diagnoses should be explored first
As discs collapse with aging, facet joints bear increasing load — from 25% to 50% of body weight by age 50
MBBs are more specific than intra-articular injection because they test the entire innervation pathway
Always check contrast before injecting anesthetic — 10-15% of the time medication is not reaching the target without it
The diagnosis must match the procedure — billing for MBBs when the suspected diagnosis is SI joint pain is a red flag
There is still a role for intra-articular facet injection therapeutically (effusions, cyst rupture)
IPSIS supplies for cervical MBBs: 25-27G spinal needles (at least 1.5 inches), microbore tubing, 1 mL and 3 mL Luer-lock syringes
IPSIS supplies for lumbar MBBs: 25-27G spinal needles (at least 3.5 inches), microbore tubing, 3 mL Luer-lock syringes
Needlecraft fundamentals: once a needle is fixed through skin and fascia, only modest trajectory changes are possible — reposition early if off-target (IPSIS)
